# Abstract

Forest managers using retention forestry need information on regeneration and
fuel development to design productive stands in fire-adapted ecosystems. We
analyzed 10-year remeasurement data from the Redwood Multiaged Experiment in
Jackson Demonstration State Forest, California. The experiment compared group
selection, aggregated retention, and low- and high-density dispersed retention
treatments and measured regeneration, sprout growth, and surface fuel loading.

Redwood regeneration responded strongly to increasing canopy openness, whereas
tanoak responses were more modest. Sprout-height findings will remain part of
the main regeneration evidence. Fuel measurements describe conditions before
and after precommercial thinning, including the PCT-associated contrast. The
manuscript will evaluate how overstory retention affects regeneration while
presenting fuel components in a form useful for integrated silviculture, fuels,
and fire management.

# Introduction

Developing and maintaining multiaged stand structures requires silvicultural
systems that create and sustain cohorts of different ages within the same stand
[@oharaSilvicultureStructuralDiversity1998; @schutzSilviculturalToolsDevelop2002].
Retention systems can retain a range of tree densities in dispersed or
aggregated patterns and can be used to maintain multiaged stands or transform
formerly even-aged stands [@mitchellRetentionSystemReconciling2002].

Coast redwood (*Sequoia sempervirens*) is well suited to this objective because
it regenerates reliably by stump sprouting and can grow beneath a retained
overstory. Its response to light is nevertheless important: reduced access to
light can limit sprout vigor and persistence
[@berrillUnderstoryLightPredicts2018; @mumaDynamicsStumpSprout2022;
@oharaUnderstoryStumpSprout2007]. Tanoak (*Notholithocarpus densiflorus*) is
also shade tolerant and a vigorous resprouter, making its response relevant to
both stand development and management of competing vegetation
[@berrillDevelopmentRedwoodRegeneration2021;
@oharaRegenerationDynamicsCoast2017].

Silvicultural decisions that promote regeneration also influence the fuel
conditions in which later management and fire occur. This paper therefore
examines regeneration under varying overstory retention and describes surface
fuel conditions before and after precommercial thinning as reference
information for integrated silvicultural, fuels, fire, and potential modeling
applications.

We use 10-year measurements from the Redwood Multiaged Experiment to evaluate
regeneration responses among retention treatments and to report fuel conditions
before and after precommercial thinning, including their PCT-associated
contrast. Redwood and tanoak provide the primary regeneration focus, with other
species retained as descriptive context where useful. Fuel components will be
presented in a publication-specific form after their analytical specification
is reviewed.


# Methods

## Study area and design

The experiment is located in the Jackson Demonstration State Forest in coastal
northern California. Four harvest treatments were replicated at four sites in
2012: group selection (GS), high-density dispersed retention (HD),
high-density aggregated retention (HA), and low-density dispersed retention
(LD). The retained-overstory treatments targeted post-harvest relative
densities of 13% or 21%; group selection created a 1-ha opening with a lightly
thinned buffer. These treatments were designed to examine alternative pathways
for developing multiaged redwood stands
[@berrillSimulatingMultiagedCoast2009; @reinekePerfectionStanddensityIndex1933].

Ten years after harvest, regeneration plots and fuel transects were established
within each 0.2-ha treatment macro plot. Regeneration measurements characterized
redwood, tanoak, and Douglas-fir; fuel transects characterized dead surface
fuels and live vegetation. The plots were remeasured after precommercial
thinning, which released selected conifers from competing trees and shrubs.

## Analysis

The final publication methods will identify the regeneration models retained
from the thesis and the revised fuel-component specifications separately. They
will define the phase-specific fuel estimates and the PCT-associated contrast,
including whether the sampling design supports a paired change analysis.
Detailed sampling procedures, model diagnostics, and expanded comparisons will
be retained as supplementary material where they are needed for reproducibility
but not for interpretation of the main findings.

For the R-D04 fuel display, treatment- and phase-specific mean loads were
estimated by averaging response-scale expectations, including modeled zeros,
over an equally weighted grid of the four study-site contexts and analytically
integrating over all fitted Gaussian random-intercept distributions. These
estimates provide model-based reference means for comparable forest conditions;
95% confidence intervals were calculated using the delta method with the full
parameter covariance, including uncertainty in random-effect variances.
Mean woody standing-vegetation reduction was estimated as the pre-PCT minus
post-PCT contrast from the matched repeated-phase model, with its joint
covariance, and interpreted as a potential surface-fuel contribution.


# Results

## Regeneration under varying overstory retention

The thesis results provide the starting material for basal area, understory
density, and sprout-height summaries. At 10 years after harvest, redwood
regeneration was greatest in the most open treatment and declined with greater
overstory retention. Tanoak responses were comparatively modest. Redwood and
tanoak sprout-height findings will remain in the main results; other species
will be retained as descriptive context where useful rather than as dedicated
main-text analyses. The final figures and summaries will retain these results
only after the publication presentation and modeling review are complete.

## Fuel conditions as reference values

Fuel conditions are reported second to support interpretation of the
silvicultural treatments and to characterize the management-relevant transition
before and after precommercial thinning. The thesis found comparatively few
treatment differences in fine dead fuels before precommercial thinning, whereas
vegetation fuels were greater in more open treatments. The publication analysis
will separate fuel components that were previously combined, report phase-
specific estimates and uncertainty, and evaluate the PCT-associated contrast.
Treatment comparisons will be retained where they clarify PCT or retained-
overstory implications.

# Discussion

The discussion will first interpret regeneration responses in relation to the
silvicultural objective of developing a new redwood cohort beneath varying
levels of retained overstory. It will then interpret phase-specific fuel
conditions and the PCT-associated contrast as a linked management question,
with conclusions limited to the reviewed sampling design and analysis.

This structure treats silviculture and fire management as linked management
questions while keeping conclusions within the support of the reviewed analyses
and cited literature.

# Supplementary material plan

Potential supplementary material includes expanded model outputs, detailed
pairwise comparisons, optional Douglas-fir detail, additional fuel-component
tables, machine-readable phase-specific estimates, supplemental figures, and
procedures that are useful for reproducibility but not essential to the main
narrative. Final contents will be chosen after the manuscript and revised fuel
analysis are settled.
